summary: This FATF report examines how criminals launder proceeds of environmental crime -- illegal logging/land clearing, illegal mining, and waste trafficking -- estimated at USD 110-281 billion annually. It finds heavy reliance on front and shell companies to co-mingle illicit and legitimate proceeds early in supply chains, trade-based fraud (false invoicing, false descriptions of goods, over/under valuation) to move money across borders, cash-intensive sectors and MVTS/hawala to pay rural labour, and offshore corporate structures with nominee/opaque beneficial owners, often enabled by corruption of officials issuing concessions and licences. It also notes convergence with tax crime, smuggling, human trafficking and, in some cases, terrorist/insurgent financing, and sets out case studies, risk indicators and priority actions for AML authorities and the private sector.

typologies.label: Third Party Payment Abuse

citations.quote: This discrepancy initiated a closer inspection of the miners and linked the group to a previous investigation had uncovered that some of the miners involved were paid by importers from South-East Asia through a scheme controlled by a network of underground exchange market dealers.
The payment would then be made either by the intermediary to the smuggler, or would come later once the intermediary got the gold to a refiner in the Middle East.
This includes integrating proceeds through third party wire transfers under the guise of payments for goods and services, but also investments and sponsorship.

typologies.review_justification: Found in Box 3.3 Brazil emeralds/hairdressers case (p.32); DRC/Rwanda gold supply chain narrative (p.22); chapter highlight (p.33). TBML008 doctrine: 'Third Party Payment Abuse settles a trade through a payer who is not the trade counterparty — an unrelated third party, split settlement, or a payment that does not match the trade. The payment breaks the link between the trade and the funds.' In the Brazil case, hairdressers were invoiced by the illegal miners 'for importing on their behalf' while the actual miners were compensated separately through an underground exchange-market network rather than directly by the Southeast Asian buyers of the emeralds -- the settlement chain deliberately does not match the underlying trade counterparties. The DRC gold example shows the same break: the intermediary, not the original smuggler/exporter, is the one who ultimately pays or is paid, consistent with the doctrine's 'payer who is not the trade counterparty' mechanism.

typologies.label: Over Invoicing

citations.quote: the trend to over or under declare goods being shipped and the use of false descriptions are common threads of both trade fraud and TBML activity

It is common for timber, processed lumber, or gold, to be exported at below market prices, change ownership and Bill of Lading en route, often in a customs free trade zone, and is imported at recipient countries at higher declared values.

typologies.review_justification: Found in Section 3.4 narrative (p.31) and Annex A 'Export & transfer pricing' indicators (p.58). TBML001 doctrine: 'the price of goods is intentionally inflated beyond their true market value.' The advisory names over-declaration explicitly as a technique distinct from the under-invoicing already claimed (TBML002U), and Annex A describes the specific mechanism of the same goods being re-declared at a higher value on the import leg after an under-valued export -- an intentional inflation of declared price beyond true market value on that leg of the transaction chain, matching TBML001's mechanism rather than the export-side under-declaration already captured.

typologies.label: Hidden Controller via Nominee Directors/Shareholders

citations.quote: These PEPs will often act as the local representatives for multinational mining ventures or as nominee directors of corporations.
These DNFBPs would identify a beneficial owner for the register, but the named individual on the registry would be a nominee with only a loose connection to the ultimate underlying owner.

The financial analysis facilitated the identification of the network and the nominees used to disguise the beneficial ownership of bank accounts and front companies as well as at least three more suspects based in Country B.

typologies.review_justification: Found in General findings on PEPs and complex structures (p.19), South American shell-company example (p.22), and Box 4.10 forestry case (p.47). PAT010 doctrine: 'identifies individuals or entities exercising effective control over an organisation despite not appearing as the declared owner, director or controller,' with indicators including 'Nominee director structure' and 'Concealed ownership arrangement.' The advisory develops this mechanism across three independent findings -- PEPs sitting as nominee directors, DNFBP-appointed nominees with only a loose connection to the true owner on beneficial ownership registries, and a case where financial analysis specifically uncovered nominees used to disguise beneficial ownership of accounts and front companies. This is control exercised behind a declared nominee, the exact PAT010 mechanism, and is distinct from the already-claimed PAT007 (network of shell companies as a structure) since the emphasis here is on the concealed controller behind each nominee, not the company network itself.

typologies.label: Layering via Nested Correspondent Activity

citations.quote: Nesting the activity within a correspondent banking relationship obscures the ultimate beneficial owner and decreases the risk of transactions associated with environmental crime being identified.

the exit of larger financial institutions and entry of smaller and/or regional institutions have the added benefit for illicit actors, of creating additional layers between the originator and the beneficiary.

typologies.review_justification: Found in Section 2.4 discussion of regional financial institutions and de-risking (p.23). BA008 doctrine: layering 'pushed through a chain of transfers designed to sever the audit trail from their source... its only job is to put distance, opacity and jurisdictional friction between the seed account and wherever the funds end up,' evidenced by 'multiple transfer hops' and a 'trail that goes cold well before it reaches an identifiable beneficial owner.' The advisory describes exactly this mechanism in the correspondent-banking context: as large banks de-risk natural-resource clients, smaller/regional institutions step in and nesting within the correspondent relationship 'creates additional layers between originator and beneficiary' and 'obscures the ultimate beneficial owner' -- the same audit-trail-severing, opacity-adding function BA008 names.

typologies.label: Informal Value Transfer (Hawala) Networks for Environmental Crime Proceeds

citations.quote: Where there is onwared smuggling to Asia, criminals often rely on informal remittance networks such as hawalas, in an effort to avoid the scrutiny of the formal financial sector.

cases show the important role of underground money value transfer services (MVTS) to facilitate laundering from environmental crimes, and particularly illegal mining. These trends are often regionally specific and reflect local informal transfer systems (e.g., "hawala").

typologies.review_justification: Found in DRC gold smuggling route narrative (p.22) and Section 3.5 chapter finding on MVTS (p.31). No existing Knowledge Centre typology matches this mechanism (best search score 0.36, against Under Invoicing, on vocabulary overlap only). The advisory develops a distinct, recurring technique: illicit gold proceeds moved onward through unlicensed hawala-style networks specifically 'to avoid the scrutiny of the formal financial sector,' confirmed as a cross-cutting finding for illegal mining laundering generally. This is a movement channel outside formal banking rails, mechanically distinct from the already-claimed cash-intensive-business front (BA007), and merits a standalone emergent entry for Knowledge Centre review.

extraction_notes: This is a broad FATF thematic report covering three distinct predicate crime types (illegal logging/land clearing, illegal mining, waste trafficking); typologies extracted are those the report develops in depth with dedicated sections/case studies rather than every risk indicator in Annex A. The 'Money Laundering from Environmental Crime' label is proposed as emergent because no existing Knowledge Centre typology captures environmental crime as the underlying predicate driver -- reviewers may wish to consider whether this should instead be modelled as a new family. The Gertler/Steinmetz/Kabila corruption cases (Annex C) are illustrative examples cited by the report rather than the report's central case studies; sanctions_desk routing reflects Gertler's Global Magnitsky designation mentioned in the text. Country list under jurisdictions covers only those tied to named cases/examples, not the full list of ~45 countries that responded to FATF's survey. Merged 5 reviewer addition(s) under schema 1.4.0; each carries its review_justification. Extraction-only record retained at data/records/.
